title: Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme
description: More than 90% of homes fitted with faulty insulation under energy-saving government schemes have not yet had repairs completed to fix the botched work
body: More than 90% of homes fitted with faulty insulation under energy-saving government schemes have not yet had repairs completed to fix the botched work, a minister has said.The government found almost all homes that had external wall insulation installed as part of two of the government's ECO schemes had defects that needed repairing.Speaking to a committee of MPs on Wednesday, Energy Minister Martin McClusky said repair works had been completed at 2,227 out of the 24,600 homes impacted.He said he was shocked by the extent of the failures and has assured affected households they would not be asked to pay to sort out these problems.McClusky told MPs the insulation schemes "didn't have correct oversight".Ofgem oversees the ECO schemes and alongside TrustMark, a government-backed consumer protection service, is responsible for auditing homes to identify faulty installations.The government and its partners have known about significant levels of defective and unsafe insulation for years, with audits finding poor work in October 2024.Ken Palfrey, a 66-year-old retired builder from Birmingham, is among the home owners waiting for repairs.He had external wall insulation installed through the ECO programme in 2024.He claims the installation was "botched", causing damage to his window sills and leading to damp and mould on his walls.He said he complained and after some months an inspection concluded the insulation had been fitted incorrectly and he was told it had to be removed immediately.Palfrey said for two years he had been on a "merry-go-round", spending "hundreds and hundreds of hours writing emails and complaining to people".Earlier this month, TrustMark referred his case to the National Energy Foundation (NEF), a charity that has funding from energy suppliers to put right damaged homes where the installer has gone out of business."It's been an absolute nightmare," Palfrey said."Every day of my life, every time you look at the insulation, you're worried about it."A TrustMark spokesperson said it was working to contact affected households and to fix "the unacceptable problems left by this faulty external wall insulation scheme". "We're sorry for what Mr Palfrey has been through and have referred him to the National Energy Foundation which should be able to get his insulation put right," the spokesperson said.Labour MP Bill Esterson, the chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, told the BBC he was seeking assurances that the victims "will be supported in a timely fashion".But he said he was concerned that Ofgem, Great Britain's energy regulator, had "failed to identify whether work had been carried out or completed to a decent standard".When asked if he had confidence in Ofgem at the committee, McClusky did not answer the question directly.He said: "There's clearly been failures in the system. We're designing a system now."He added Ofgem was a "very different organisation than it was a number of years ago".A spokesperson for Ofgem said: "It is unacceptable that households have been left with substandard ECO4 work. Ofgem was not responsible for assuring the quality of installations."The spokesperson said the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) "is responsible for the design and overall outcomes of ECO, and that Ofgem's role did not include assessing installation quality"."Our role, set by government, is to administer the scheme and hold suppliers to account for meeting their obligations," the Ofgem spokesperson added. "When serious quality problems emerged, we went beyond our core role to support affected households and help establish the scale of the problem."The BBC has asked TrustMark for comment.The two ECO schemes that have caused widespread issues are known as ECO4 and Great British Insulation Scheme (GBIS).ECO4 was launched in 2022 and since then, more than 300,000 homes have had heat pumps, solar panels and insulation fitted under the £4bn scheme. It is closing in December.GBIS - which opened in 2023 and has now closed - was more narrowly designed to help households lower their energy bills by installing cheap insulation.The BBC has been reporting on the impact of faulty insulation installed under these schemes in recent years.Fuel Poverty Action, a campaign group, argues that problems with faulty upgrades under a range of government energy efficiency schemes could be affecting as many as 100,000 homes."Ignoring the other defective measures is shockingly negligent, and is causing huge harm," said Jonathan Bean, policy lead at Fuel Poverty Action."Defective internal wall insulation causes major hidden damage, making it a ticking time bomb in homes."The government estimates that 29% of it is defective but chose not to include it in the Find and Fix process."A spokesperson for DESNZ said: "We inherited the failing ECO4 scheme, which we ended after it clearly let families down."No household should have to pay to put the issues right and TrustMark is working to support those affected to ensure this is the case."Our Warm Homes Plan will overhaul the system to protect consumers and ensure failings are not repeated."

schema.headline: Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme

title: Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
description: "We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn
body: "We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening."We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.While she seemed fine at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.An ultrasound before her death showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine. A zookeeper said surgery was not an option for full-grown hippos and "our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own".The zoo also tried a different approach to attempt to get the hat to pass by encouraging Fiona to stand on a vibration plate platform borrowed from a local horse farm."Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her.  They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said. Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.Her death is also very premature, with hippos normally living up to 50 years in human care, according to the zoo."Although this was not an intentional incident, of which, regrettably, there are many, Fiona's painful death is a tragic reminder that everyone should behave carefully and respectfully around animals," Debbie Metzler, the Managing Director of Captive Wildlife for the animal rights group Peta. "Peta expects that the zoo will review its protocols to help prevent anything like this from happening again, and we urge every visitor to secure their belongings and never toss objects near an animal's enclosure."As well as being famous online, Fiona's story inspired an ice cream flavour and a character in Cincinnati's ballet.Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval said Fiona "was a symbol of perseverance and joy" in the city."She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world," he wrote on X. "Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."

schema.headline: Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo

title: William and Catherine's India tour was 'particularly special', aide says
description: Image source, PAByDaniela RelphSenior royal correspondentThe most senior advisor to the Prince of Wales has said this week's visit with the Princess o
body: Image source, PAByDaniela RelphSenior royal correspondentThe most senior advisor to the Prince of Wales has said this week's visit with the Princess of Wales to India was "particularly special" and described the royal couple "as very much a team".Prince William and Catherine are now back in the UK after spending three days in Mumbai and Delhi - the first time they have travelled together on overseas royal duties since the princess's cancer treatment.The visit focused on the prince's Earthshot Prize which were hosted in Mumbai. His wife last attended the Earthshot awards when they were held in Boston in 2022."The prince has really enjoyed having the princess alongside him for Earthshot, and for her to see first-hand how much it has grown in scale since she last attended in Boston," Ian Patrick, the prince's private secretary told reporters."She's enormously proud of what he's achieved, and it has been particularly special for them to experience this moment together. They are very much a team."The prince and princess also met the Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at his residence in Delhi where they discussed UK-India partnerships.In a social media post after the meeting, the prime minister said it had been "a pleasure to meet their Royal Highnesses" and praised the Earthshot Prize for "showcasing Indian ingenuity in addressing global environmental challenges".The meeting was a late addition to the prince and princess's plans. Prime Minister Modi altered his schedule to return to India from a summit in the Philippines to ensure he could meet the royal couple."The prince and princess have had a thoroughly enjoyable time in India. They've been incredibly touched by the warmth of the welcome they've received," said Patrick.Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, William and Catherine's India visit was their first overseas trip together since Catherine's cancer treatmentThe couple were last in India for an official tour in 2016."It's been wonderful for them to return together after ten years," the private secretary said. "They were incredibly inspired by the people they met. They leave with very happy memories and a real enthusiasm for building on the connections they've made with the next generation."There was a focus on young people and their potential during the three day visit. This year, for the first time, there was a Children's Earthshot Awards where 15,000 schools across India took part creating solutions for environmental problems in their own communities."We cannot look into the eyes of the next generation and tell them that we knew what was happening, we knew what was at stake, and yet we did not do everything in our power to change it," Prince William said in his speech at the Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony. "They will not judge us by the promises we made, but by the world we leave behind."Figure caption, Watch: Catherine visited a maternity hospital in Mumbai on the last day of royal visit"The prince and princess don't want young people to feel unheard or that the challenges facing the planet and society are beyond their control," said Patrick. "They want them to feel optimistic, empowered and part of the solutions."The Earthshot Prize was designed as a ten-year project - it is now in its sixth year and Prince William remains ambitious for it."Companies including Amazon, IKEA, Nvidia, Standard Chartered and Uber are now stepping forward to help their impact spread even further," said Jason Knauf, the chief executive officer of the Earthshot Prize. "This is enormously encouraging but the prince wants to see more of the world's biggest businesses and investors get involved... every business and investor who joins us helps these solutions grow faster, building a healthier, happier and more prosperous future for us all."Now that the prince and princess are travelling together on international duty, the visit was an insight into way their royal trips will operate in future.Figure caption, What did we learn from Kate and William’s India trip?The days of royal tours lasting two weeks will not be the approach of the royal couple who think they make a big impact over shorter trips with the additional help of social media to amplify their engagements. They also want to limit the amount of time they spend away from their three children."The prince and princess want their overseas travel to have purpose, meaning and impact. It's about building stronger relationships, creating opportunities for collaboration and supporting projects that deliver real results," explained Patrick.Despite plans to keep future royal tours short, it's believed a visit to Australia could be in the plans for the couple in 2027.At the Earthshot Prize Awards ceremony on Tuesday, Prince William was heard by reporters saying "Big year next year, Australia!"Kensington Palace has not yet confirmed any further travel plans for the Waleses. They last visited Australia in 2014 with nine-month-old Prince George. It is possible that their three children could join them on a future Australia trip.Additional reporting by Charlotte Scarr in Delhi

schema.headline: William and Catherine's India tour was 'particularly special', aide says

title: Why children lie and it is important they do
description: Why fibbing about stolen snacks is an important part of childhoodImage source, Elena HoickaImage caption, Prof Hoicka's daughter Ada tries to sneakily
body: Why fibbing about stolen snacks is an important part of childhoodImage source, Elena HoickaImage caption, Prof Hoicka's daughter Ada tries to sneakily eat cookie dough aged two when she thought her mum wasn't lookingByGeorge SandemanWhen drawings appear on the wall or biscuits disappear from the tin, your child might blame the dog or claim there was a ghost - even if they are clutching crayons or covered in crumbs.Children telling fibs is something most parents experience, but such dishonesty and deception is an important part of mental development. "It's actually a skill that they're developing and that they will play with in order to get better," clinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern tells the CBeebies Parenting Download podcast. Here, experts explain why learning to lie is a sign of healthy behaviour - and how to help encourage honesty.Image source, Elena HoickaImage caption, Prof Hoicka's daughter Juno also deceives her aged three by hiding under a table to eat marshmallowsYoung children aren't quite sophisticated enough to lie, says Redfern, but they are capable of deception before the age of one. One of the studies mentioned on the podcast comes from the University of Bristol, external, which found that around a quarter of children appear to understand some form of deception by the time they are 10 months old. Prof Elena Hoicka, who led the study, says it was fascinating to see how "surprisingly young" kids could be so adept and cunning, including her own."As a mother of three, I can certainly vouch for how artful and wily they can be. "Hiding under the table or in the bathroom to eat sweets or chocolate is their common ploy."Hoicka says that the kind of deception a child uses from the age of two is quite basic - like pretending not to hear their parent or denying they've done something.CBeebies Parenting DownloadClinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern explains why young children may lie and Traitors winner Rachel Duffy discusses how she encourages hers to tell the truth"It could also extend to doing forbidden activities in secret," she says. "For example, looking in a bag they were told not to look in when no one is apparently watching, or making excuses, such as claiming to need the toilet when asked to tidy up."By the age of three, they have become much more proficient and creative in their deceptions, showing a deeper understanding of language and how other people's minds work.She says they also start to withhold information. For instance, truthfully telling their parents that their sibling has hit them but omitting the fact that they hit their sibling first.These deceptions are a sign of them developing something Redfern calls "theory of mind".Image source, Elena HoickaImage caption, Ada, age two, deceives her mum by hiding in the bathroom to eat chocolate she had stolen"As children grow up, we want them to learn and develop the skill that they are their own human being with a separate mind and intentions," she explains."This is how [they] develop the skills in empathy, or being able to think about another person's thoughts and feelings that might differ from their own."Another reason a child might lie is self-preservation as they don't want to upset or disappoint their parent."All human beings are driven by attachment," says Redfern. "[Children are] driven by being able to preserve that relationship with their caregivers as they depend upon it."Early on, they learn what brings them closer to their caregiver and what pulls them apart, she says. With this in mind, Redfern thinks you can encourage honesty by creating a safe environment for a child to tell the truth."[We] have to think about ways we can help children feel safe enough to tell us the truth [when] they've made a mistake... and they don't want to disappoint us."This is something Rachel Duffy, who won the latest series of The Traitors, tells the CBeebies Parenting podcast that she has been trying to do.Image source, Elena HoickaImage caption, Prof Hoicka with her daughters Ada, now aged six, and Juno who is three years oldThe mum-of-three recalls one occasion when her eldest son borrowed his brother's bike and broke it after crashing it into a car. Initially, he tried to lie about what happened."I said to him, 'You'll not get into big trouble when you tell me the truth.' I just left and gave him a little space."And he went, 'Yeah, that was me.' And then he knew that space was safe. We had a conversation - no raised voices, no roaring or shouting."Redfern says this is a good example of how to deal with such a situation and that there are occasions when a lie, or nuance, might be appropriate - such as when they receive a gift they don't want or describe other people physically."My kids delightfully told me recently that I was very wrinkly," she says. "Again, I try to take it with open curiosity."She does this by talking about why they think she is wrinkly. "I think just being able to explore as children get older, just having open, curious conversations - it really develops empathy for somebody else's feelings when they've been shown and modelled empathy over and over again."

schema.headline: Why children lie and it is important they do

title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByHelen BushbyCulture reporterFlorence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByHelen BushbyCulture reporterFlorence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery. The actress wrote on Instagram, external how "stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend". "I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pugh has spoken out before about judgement about how women look Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds"."The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg."Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming". "I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again"."I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism, external, which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'. "A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick. "We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pugh is no stranger to a striking red carpet outfit Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.In 2024, she told the Times, external she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived"."Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance. "I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said. "But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.  'Please be gentle'Pugh also said she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs."I was... horrified," she wrote, claiming the articles had damaged her reputation.The actress concluded by urging followers to think about their attitudes towards physical appearance."I understand that we are in a warped part of image history right now, with beauty standards changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with," she said. "But please be gentle to yourselves and others when you go in on people's physical appearance."I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at the situation that's being projected onto us."It feels inescapable, but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye."

schema.headline: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation

title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
description: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example,
body: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said.Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

schema.headline: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force

title: Girls as young as five targeted for upskirting as charges continue to rise
description: Girls as young as five have been targeted for upskirting, new police figures show. Over the past three years, Wales' four forces received 219 complain
body: Girls as young as five have been targeted for upskirting, new police figures show. Over the past three years, Wales' four forces received 219 complaints from females up to the age of 87, with 18 people charged, results of Freedom of Information (FOI) requests, external reveal. Upskirting involves taking a photo or video, external beneath someone's clothing - without their knowledge - with the intention of viewing their genitals, buttocks or underwear. It was made a criminal offence under the Voyeurism (Offences) Act 2019, external and carries a maximum sentence of two years in prison.The Crown Prosecution Service, external urged people to report incidents immediately, saying those that led to charges almost doubled between 2022 and 2026."As well as being an extremely damaging offence in its own right, our prosecutors often see upskirting forming part of a wider pattern of sexual offending," said national lead for sexual offence prosecutions Siobhan Blake.Between January 2023 and June 2026, Wales' four police forces received 219 complaints, with the highest being 159 in the Dyfed-Powys area and the lowest, six in Gwent, according to the FOI figures.Where ages were recorded, 11 involved under-10s, 67 came from girls aged 11 to 17, 35 from those 18 to 24, and 12 from over-55s.From these 219 complaints, nine people were charged in the north Wales force area, six in Dyfed-Powys, three in south Wales, while Gwent had no data.A previous FOI to Greater Manchester Police, external showed it received 146 reports between 2019 and 2025, leading to 41 arrests and 10 people being charged.West Midlands Police received 75 reports between 2022 and 2026, with 23 charged, according to another FOI, external. "I think a lot of the time [boys] think it's a joke or banter, but it's not funny," said student Rowan Stanger, 21. "Whilst it is illegal, I don't think a lot of people take it seriously."She was in secondary school when it was made a criminal offence in Wales and England in 2019, and as a teenager, heard about lots of cases of it happening to friends. "I was wearing shorts under skirts in school, I think that's what was kind of expected even before I really knew why," she added."That is still ingrained in me. I'll rarely wear one without."Rowan is part of a student-led Time to Act, which fights against sexual violence in higher education.Emily Hasling, 23, is also part of the Cardiff-based campaign group, and said she remembers when she was in university and going to nightclubs, she would only wear jeans. "Young boys don't see it as sexual assault or sexual violence, because it's not a physical kind of touching element, it's a photo," she said."So that's how they see it 'just a photo'." Another group member Freya Price, 22, described feeling wary on public transport. "Obviously trains are quite crowded so if I can't stand in a corner I'll feel quite anxious, because I can't guarantee that someone's not going to violate my privacy," she said. Olivia (not her real name), a teenager from south Wales, said she loves wearing skirts but from an early age has been made to feel uncomfortable in them.She described how boys in primary school had an obsession with "flipping up girls' skirts", which led to them either wearing shorts underneath or switching to trousers. This was her first experience of feeling unsafe in them, while she was then upskirted on a night out while at university."There was a little stage area and I'm dancing, having a great time," Olivia said. "I look over to my right and someone has got a camera with the flash on underneath my skirt."We made eye contact and he walked off. I was frozen and I didn't know if I was imagining it. I didn't know if I could tell someone or who to tell."She has not felt comfortable enough to wear the same dress again until recently, describing her head as being "on a swivel" every time she was in a club, and feeling like she could not get too drunk. In 2019, Libby Squire, 21, was raped and murdered by Pawel Relowicz, who was found to have previous convictions for voyeurism and public sex acts.Libby's mother Lisa Squire has spent the past five years trying to increase the reporting of non-contact sexual offences, launching the It Does Matter campaign in 2024."I know first hand how harmful behaviours that are too often dismissed as 'minor' can build into something catastrophic, and I am committed to ensuring no other family experiences what we have," she said. The NSPCC said its Childline service, external has heard from young people who have had indecent images of them taken and shared."They tell us how devastating the abuse can be on their mental and emotional wellbeing, leaving them afraid, ashamed and unsure where to turn," a spokesperson said. One 16-year-old described how the same boy tripped her up on the way to her seat every day in her tutor group, laughing and looking up her skirt."It just freaks me out and I don't know what to do about it," she said.A mum called to say her daughter, also 16, had heard a rumour a boy in her year had taken a photograph up her skirt, and shared it with his friends.She added: "The thought alone is incredibly upsetting for her."The Children's Commissioner for England said Children's Commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza said: "The fact a number of teachers have admitted or been found guilty of upskirting offences, some in their own classrooms, is particularly shocking. "Teachers and other school professionals have a clear responsibility to keep children safe, so staff must be alert to the signs of sexual harassment and abuse and ensure all children know where they can turn for help and support if an incident occurs."If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC Action Line

schema.headline: Girls as young as five targeted for upskirting as charges continue to rise

title: Mykhailo Mudryk: Andriy Shevchenko disputes player's doping claims
description: Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federatio
body: Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk firmly placed the blame for his 20-month absence from the sport on his national association, which has led to Shevchenko's response.In a statement, former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko, who is now president of the UAF, said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally" and called on the player to retract his words.He added: "His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample. "The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work."He added that "numerous investigations and audits" undertaken as part of the case were unable to shed light on when or where the substance entered Mudryk's system.In his interview Mudryk also claimed Shevchenko had offered him little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and said its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.However, Shevchenko went on to say that national team staff had complied with a request from Chelsea not to provide Mudryk with any medication while on international duty. And he also challenged the former Shakhtar Donetsk forward to provide evidence "to back up his words"."Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps," Shevchenko added."These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine."The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case."I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism. "If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question."BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk's representatives for comment.

schema.headline: Mykhailo Mudryk: Andriy Shevchenko disputes player's doping claims

title: Jeremy Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
description: The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a h
body: The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a high bar of proof.That is why it has taken so long for the ICJ to deliver a ruling that genocide has been committed.In an ideal world for lawyers and investigators, they would assemble evidence from government documents and military orders. In practice, that is hard if not impossible to get.Governments harbouring genocidal intent do not publicise their objectives. Instead, the Court has inferred evidence of genocidal intent from the actions taken by Myanmar's security forces and local militias against the Rohingya people.According to Janina Dill, Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government of the University of Oxford, "Genocidal intent can be inferred from a pattern of conduct… It does not mean the commission of atrocities had to follow only one goal, genocide. If that were the case, demonstrating that atrocities also followed other goals (like counterinsurgency, punishment or displacement) would negate genocidal intent."The court was incredibly clear that these are plausible goals, but it ruled that the totality of the evidence cannot be explained without genocide being one objective."In other words, even if a state has been attacked, and if it orders its forces on to the offensive claiming self-defence, the sum of its actions could add up to genocide.The justices made clear that each case needed to be treated on its merits. But because the court's decisions affect the way the law is interpreted, the Myanmar case does have an impact on the other genocide cases that are being heard by the ICJ. The most prominent is the one brought by South Africa against Israel over the killing and destruction it has inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza.The British barrister, Philippe Sands KC, part of the Gambia's legal team, was in the chamber of the ICJ in The Hague to hear the verdict. Sands told the BBC's World at One programme that when they were arguing the case against Myanmar at the ICJ in January this year, Gaza was "the elephant in the room. Everybody knew that the court's approach in this case would have implications in the next one".The approach taken by the ICJ justices in the judgement on Myanmar, he told the BBC, clarifies the standard of evidence they require to prove genocide."If the Gambia had lost, South Africa's case would, in effect, be over."But the Gambia now having succeeded, the door remains open for South Africa. That doesn't mean that South Africa will win. It doesn't mean that the International Court of Justice will find there was a genocide in Gaza. It means that the evidentiary standard has been defined very clearly, and it will be now for the parties in that next case and in other cases to meet those standards."The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade.The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas.That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court.The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimes… we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity".It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.  Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide".Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ.He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case.She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

schema.headline: Jeremy Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications

title: Don't buy smart glasses, Dutch data watchdog advises
description: The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wro
body: The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent, or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment. Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings. But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.In February, reports revealed outsourced workers were able to view sensitive content recorded on Meta smart glasses Meta said at the time such workers might sometimes review content, including video and images, in order to help improve its AI.It said it took the protection of people's data very seriously, and was constantly refining its efforts and tools in that area, and would filter it first to blur faces in images.The AP investigation was not primarily focused on data protection - instead it was concerned with algorithms and AI.In the UK Paul Arnold, chief executive of privacy watchdog the Information Commission, who has a severe visual impairment has previously stressed the complexity of the argument, external around smart glasses."They can help me and others better understand our surroundings, access information and navigate the world with greater confidence," he wrote in September.But he said he had been "shocked and appalled by some of the irresponsible and harmful ways people are using these technologies".

schema.headline: Don't buy smart glasses, Dutch data watchdog advises

title: GTA 6 breaks records as sales top $2.3bn - industry estimate
description: Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.The research firm said its e
body: Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.Around three quarters of the game's sales have been for the PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn, adjusted for inflation.Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.

schema.headline: GTA 6 breaks records as sales top $2.3bn - industry estimate

title: Thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret operation
description: A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses,
body: A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies.It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.The security threat was discovered by ethical hackers at a firm called Omega Systems - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm.The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week."It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named."From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impactedOn 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targetedOn 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium and Luxembourg the worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impactedThe waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites."These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners."There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay. "This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM. He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included dismantling our hardware"."In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.RDM confirmed that there was no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continued to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.

schema.headline: Thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret operation

title: Mauricio Pochettino: Man Utd boss priorities include Fernandes, culture and defence
description: "We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."Mauricio Pochettino has used his first
body: "We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?There is a clear non-negotiable."To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to."It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club."We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure."Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.Then there is Dalot.The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude. Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.There is one issue Pochettino mentioned in his interview he will soon discover requires delicate handling.United's match-going fans have stood by every manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired. There is no reason to think that will change now.However, their relationship with the club's ownership is fractured, possibly beyond repair. Fresh accounts to 30 September show the club's overall debt remains more than £1.1bn and a further £14.5m was spent on finance costs in the previous quarter. This fuels discontent in the stands, already heightened because of various ticketing measures, none of which are viewed by most supporters as being positive."We need to be united," said Pochettino."Chemistry is really important, chemistry between us and the staff and the fans and the players, the directors, the owners and everything."

schema.headline: Mauricio Pochettino: Man Utd boss priorities include Fernandes, culture and defence

title: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
description: Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agree
body: Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum. A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday."There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said."But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow."So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes. An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling. Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU. However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU. He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost". She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc. Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough"."We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

schema.headline: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
